draft.title: Changing models of the atom
card: Dalton
In the early 1800s, John Dalton pictured atoms as tiny solid balls with nothing inside them. Each element had its own kind of ball.
Thomson
In 1897, J. J. Thomson found tiny negative particles inside atoms, now called electrons. His model showed an atom as a positive ball with electrons spread through it.
Rutherford
In 1911, Rutherford's team fired particles at thin gold foil. Most went straight through, but a few bounced back. This showed an atom has a tiny, dense, positive nucleus and is mostly empty space.
Bohr
In 1913, Niels Bohr said electrons move around the nucleus in set shells. A model changes when new experiments give evidence that it cannot explain.
draft.remember: Each new model of the atom was built to fit new experimental evidence.

a.q: Why did scientists change the model of the atom over time?
opts: New experiments gave evidence the old model could not fit
Older scientists were proven to have made no observations
Atoms themselves changed their structure over the years
Newer models were simply drawn with more detail and colour
a.why: A model is kept only while it fits the evidence. When new experiments showed something it could not explain, scientists changed the model. Atoms themselves did not change, only our ideas about them.

b.q: In Rutherford's gold foil experiment, most particles passed straight through the foil but a few bounced back. What did this show?
opts: Atoms are mostly empty space with a tiny dense nucleus
Atoms are solid balls with nothing inside them
Atoms are positive balls with electrons spread through
Electrons move around the nucleus in set shells
b.why: Most particles went through, so atoms are mostly empty space. A few bounced back, so there must be a tiny, dense, positive centre. The solid ball and spread-out electron models could not explain these results.
b.clue: What would make a few particles bounce back?

a.best: New experiments gave evidence the old model could not fit

b.best: Atoms are mostly empty space with a tiny dense nucleus

problems.detail: Why (a) says 'A model is kept only while it fits the evidence'. That is more absolute than the card, which only says a model changes when new evidence cannot be explained. Models with known limits, such as Bohr's, are still kept and used.
